title: 4B Setup
teaches: The 4B- (Stan Weinstein) as we trade it: after a Stage 4 decline under a falling 30-week line, a stock that has seen its low for the cycle sets a higher low on drying volume, reclaims the 50-day and pauses above it with room to run, the buy is the trade through the pause high at market once price is back above the 200-day and never more than 4% past it, the trade is short term, with the first sell a judgment on day 3 or later, the full size at one price and no add in the plan, and a plain 4B that is still falling is much too soon to buy.

walkthroughs.title: NUS, April 2013: the longest base
steps: NUS, 2013. A December capitulation low, then a February higher low, with the 150 and 200-day flat for three months.
Then a 19-day pause above a turning 50-day. The low was 48% under its high; now it's back above the 200-day.
April 18 it trades over the pause high. Buy at market, 49.99. Stop 49.05, a tight 1.9%.
If Stage 4 resumes, the stop takes you out. Instead its best run hit 31.9R. Sell into a push, trail the rest.

walkthroughs.title: PENN, November 2019: the picture-book shape
steps: Memorize this shape. PENN, 2019: a long Stage 4 under a falling 30-week line, then an August low.
In October, a higher low 7.7% above it. Then a 17-day pause above a 50-day that's turned up.
November 5 it trades over the pause high, above the 200-day. Buy at market, 22.12. Stop 21.49, 2.8% away.
If it stalls under a falling long average, the stop goes. Instead its best run was 15.7R. Sell into a push.

walkthroughs.title: F, February 2024: the planned loss
steps: A 4B- can be right and still lose. Ford, 2024: down 37.5% to 9.63, then a higher low 3.6% above it.
It's 70 sessions off the low. A 12-day pause above the 50-day, and the trigger day closes near its high.
February 12 it trades over the pause high. Buy at market, 12.99. Stop 12.59, 3.1% away.
Next day it drops to 12.48 and the stop's gone. A planned 3.1% loss. The stop did its job.

questions.q: Your stock keeps sliding under a falling 30-week line. Weinstein's legend calls that a plain 4B. What's it telling you?
choices: Too soon to buy, it's still falling
The bottom's in, buy the strength
Early in the drop, sell the rallies
It's a Stage 2 breakout on volume
questions.answer: Too soon to buy, it's still falling
questions.why: Too soon. Weinstein's legend reads a plain 4B as late in the downtrend, much too soon to consider buying. Late can still mean another leg lower, and nobody knows where it stops. There's no low yet, so there's nothing for you to risk against. The one we trade is the 4B-, with the minus, and even that waits for its base. While it's in Stage 4, there's no reason to own it.
questions.lesson_line: A plain 4B is still falling. Wait for the minus.

wrong.The bottom's in, buy the strength: That's what the minus says, not a plain 4B. A plain 4B hasn't shown you a low yet.
wrong.Early in the drop, sell the rallies: The B means late in the decline, not early.
wrong.It's a Stage 2 breakout on volume: Stage 2 is the uptrend. A 4B is still inside the Stage 4 decline.

questions.simple: A plain 4B is late in a falling trend. It's much too soon to buy.

questions.q: Weinstein's legend also has a 4B-, with a minus on the end. What's that minus telling you about the stock?
choices: It has now seen its low for the cycle
It's still falling, just slower
It's already in a Stage 2 uptrend
It's a short, the decline isn't done
questions.answer: It has now seen its low for the cycle
questions.why: It has seen its low for the cycle. That's the minus in Weinstein's legend. It isn't officially in Stage 1A yet, but the low is in. Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say buy now. The low being in just puts it on your radar. The buy still waits for a higher low and a pause above the averages, so you risk against a real level instead of guessing at a bottom.
questions.lesson_line: The minus says the low is in. The buy comes later.

wrong.It's still falling, just slower: Still falling is the plain 4B. The minus says the low is in.
wrong.It's already in a Stage 2 uptrend: Not even close. It isn't officially in Stage 1A yet, let alone Stage 2.
wrong.It's a short, the decline isn't done: The minus says the opposite. The low for the cycle is in.

questions.simple: The minus says the low is in. It doesn't say buy yet.

reasons: one web publisher (stageanalysis.net) plus the card's own line

questions.q: A 4B- only comes after a Stage 4 decline. The 30-week line was falling, with price stuck under it.
questions.why: True. No decline, no 4B-. This setup is a turn after a real Stage 4, the 30-week line rolling over and price stuck under it. Check that line at the low. If it was still rising when the low hit, you're looking at a pullback in an uptrend. That's a different trade with different rules. Name the stage right and you'll manage the trade right.
questions.lesson_line: No Stage 4 first, no 4B-.
questions.simple: True. A 4B- comes after a real decline, with the 30-week line falling and price under it.

reasons: the 20-session test is the card's own working rule

questions.q: Weinstein works off weekly charts and you trade a daily. Tap the daily average that stands in for his 30-week line.
questions.sentence: The 30-week line is about the ___-day average.
questions.why: 150. Thirty weeks of five sessions is about 150 days, so the 150-day stands in for his 30-week line. His 40-week line is the 200-day the same way. It's close, not exact, and that's fine. You need it to read his stages on the daily chart you actually trade off.
questions.lesson_line: Thirty weeks is about 150 days. Forty weeks is about 200.
questions.simple: The 30-week line is about the 150-day average on a daily chart.

reasons: the TraderLion archive page (x05) could not be opened to re-check; Deepvue (x04) was confirmed

questions.q: A 4B- is a short-term trade on our trims, not a ride into Stage 2 with adds along the way.
questions.why: True. It is a short-term trade on the house trims: one price, one stop, no adding along the way.
questions.lesson_line: In and out on our trims. One price, one stop, no adds.

questions.q: On a 4B-, the stock has to close back above its 50-day before you even think about buying it.
questions.why: True. Winning back the 50-day is the first real sign buyers have taken over. It's the recapture the whole setup hangs on. Under the line, sellers still own it and every rally runs into them. Even then it isn't the buy. I want to see it pause above the 50-day, then trade through that pause high.
questions.lesson_line: Win back the 50-day first. Then we talk about a buy.
questions.simple: True. It has to win back the 50-day first, and the buy comes after a pause above it.

reasons: one cited fact only (the criteria card)

questions.q: We do not buy a 4B- while the close is still under the 200-day.
questions.why: True. No longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day, no long. Get back above it first.

questions.q: You're marking up a 4B- chart. Which low do you mark as the cycle low, the one everything else gets measured from?
choices: The lowest low of the whole decline
The most recent dip on the chart
The low of the first big down day
Wherever the 50-day turned up
questions.answer: The lowest low of the whole decline
questions.why: The lowest low of the whole decline. That's the bottom of Stage 4, the price the stock hasn't been back to since. Mark it first. The higher low, how far it fell off its highs, and the call that the low is in all measure off it. If price ever closes back under it, the call was wrong and you start the count over.
questions.lesson_line: Mark the cycle low first. Everything else measures off it.

wrong.The most recent dip on the chart: A recent dip may be your higher low. The cycle low is the bottom of the whole decline.
wrong.The low of the first big down day: That's one day early in the slide. The stock went lower after it.
wrong.Wherever the 50-day turned up: The 50-day turns well after the low. You want the price low itself.

questions.simple: Mark the lowest low of the whole decline. Everything else is measured from that price.

reasons: one cited fact only (the criteria card)
a proposed number the owner may change
fixed before

questions.q: What is the smallest step above the cycle low that counts as a higher low?
questions.why: 3%. A higher low sits at least 3% above the cycle low. It comes at least 10 sessions after the low, after a rally of 5% or more. These are our working numbers. An equal low is not a higher low.
questions.lesson_line: A higher low is a real step up, not a tie.

wrong.1%: 1% is too small. Our working rule needs at least 3% above the cycle low.
wrong.5%: 5% is the rally needed before the higher low, a separate test. The step itself needs at least 3%.
wrong.10%: 10 is the number of sessions the higher low waits after the cycle low, not a percent.

questions.simple: The smallest step that counts is 3% above the cycle low, so a real step up counts and a tie does not.

reasons: one cited fact only (the criteria card)
a proposed number the owner may change
fixed before

questions.q: Your stock just closed back over its 50-day for the first time in months. Why not just buy that close?
choices: You want it to pause and hold first
No reason, buy it right there
Volume has to double first
The 200-day has to turn up first
questions.answer: You want it to pause and hold first
questions.why: You want a pause first. The first close over the 50-day is often just a pop. Plenty of them fail the next day and you're back under the line. A few days holding above it tells you the reclaim is real. It also builds a small range: a high to trigger on and a low to risk against. That's a tight, honest stop instead of a guess.
questions.lesson_line: The reclaim puts it on your list. The pause makes it a trade.

wrong.No reason, buy it right there: A first close over the line can fail the next day. And we buy through a trigger during the day, not at the close.
wrong.Volume has to double first: Volume raises the grade. It's not a must, and doubling is no rule of ours.
wrong.The 200-day has to turn up first: A turning 200-day is a nice cue, not the gate. The pause is what you're waiting on.

questions.simple: Wait for a pause above the 50-day. It shows the reclaim holds and gives you a tight stop.

reasons: one cited source only (the criteria card)
a proposed number the owner may change
fixed before

questions.q: A 4B- sets up in a $5 stock that trades $20 million a day. The chart is perfect. We can take it.
questions.why: False. We only trade stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. This one has the dollar volume and fails on price. Cheap stocks swing hard on nothing and gap right through stops. A perfect chart doesn't change that. Both tests have to pass, so go find a name we'd actually own.
questions.lesson_line: Under $10 is out, however clean the base.
questions.simple: False. A $5 stock is under our $10 floor, however good the chart looks.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: This is the day before the trigger. It's back over the 50-day and pausing. How do you get in?
choices: Market order through the pause high
On the first close over the 50-day
A limit order resting at the pause high
On a close back over the 200-day
questions.answer: Market order through the pause high
questions.why: Market order as it trades through the pause high. That high is where the sellers in the pause kept turning it back. When price takes it out during the day, they're used up, and you want in right there. Set an alert on the pause high the night before. We buy with a market order, because a limit can leave you watching it run. Your stop goes a few cents under the low of the day, the LOD.
questions.lesson_line: Alert on the pause high. Market order when it trades through.

wrong.On the first close over the 50-day: That close is the reclaim, step one. The buy waits for the pause and a trade through its high.
wrong.A limit order resting at the pause high: We buy at market. A limit can leave you watching it run without you.
wrong.On a close back over the 200-day: Being over the 200-day is a gate, not the trigger. And we buy during the day, never at the close.

questions.simple: Buy at market as it trades through the pause high. Set the alert the night before.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57)
the trigger is a held decision (D-003)
fixed before

questions.story: Months of decline, a higher low, the 50-day won back, and a pause sitting above it.

questions.q: A long Stage 4 slide, then a small, quick base with price still under falling averages. Buying that is getting in too early.
questions.why: True. A big decline leaves a lot of trapped holders above. A small base right off the low hasn't worked through them yet, and price is often still under falling averages. I'd rather give it time. Let it build a higher low, win back the 50-day and pause. You'll buy a little higher, but against a level that's been tested.
questions.lesson_line: Big decline, small base: too early. Give it time.
questions.simple: True. A quick little base after a big drop is often too early, so give it time.

deeper.trap: Time alone isn't the test either. A base can be old and still have no higher low. You want the higher low, the 50-day won back and the pause, not a day count.

reasons: a proposed number the owner may change
the web source supports only the idea, not the number
fixed before

questions.q: You bought this trigger at 22.12 with your stop at 21.49. Where's 3R?
questions.why: 24.01. Start with one R, your risk per share: 22.12 minus 21.49 is 0.63. Three of those is 1.89. Add it to the 22.12 buy and 3R sits at 24.01. Mark it so you know what the trade is doing. It's a ruler, not a sell order. Our first sell is a judgment, often into a push on day 3 or later. This was PENN in November 2019.
questions.lesson_line: Know where 3R is before the open. It's a ruler, not a sell order.
questions.simple: 3R is your buy plus three times your risk per share. Here that's 24.01.

reasons: a computed key
the 3R trim is the owner's hard rule (B19)

wrong.$23.38: That's three R added to the stop, not the buy.
wrong.$22.75: That's only one R above the buy.

questions.story: A long Stage 4, an October higher low, then a 17-day pause over a 50-day that turned up. You're in.

questions.q: A stock topped at 60.00 and bottomed at 31.50 on the slide. How far off its high did it get?
questions.why: 47.5%. The drop is 60.00 minus 31.50, which is 28.5. Divide that by the 60.00 high, not the low, and you get 47.5%. We read every chart in percents. Nearly half off its high tells you how hard it was sold and how many holders are trapped above. Those holders are who sells into your rally later.
questions.lesson_line: Measure from the high: the drop over the high.
questions.simple: Take the drop of 28.5 and divide by the high of 60.00. That's 47.5% off the high.

reasons: one cited fact only (the criteria card)
a computed key
the depth threshold is held (D-070) and is not used here

wrong.52.5%: That's where the low sits as a share of the high, not the drop.
wrong.90.5%: You divided the drop by the low instead of the high.
wrong.190.5%: You divided the high by the low and forgot to take away one.

questions.q: The cycle low is 20.00 and the higher low is 21.40. How far above the cycle low is it, in percent?
questions.why: The step up is 21.40 minus 20.00. Divide it by the cycle low of 20.00 to get 7.0%. Our working rule wants at least 3%, so this clears it. It also needs to be set at least 10 sessions after the low, after a rally of 5% or more.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the step up from the cycle low.
questions.simple: The higher low is 7.0% above the cycle low, which clears our 3% minimum.

reasons: one cited fact only (the criteria card)
a computed key
fixed before

wrong.6.5%: Divided the step up by the higher low instead of the cycle low.
wrong.0.07%: Forgot to multiply by one hundred.
wrong.107.0%: Gave the higher low as a share of the cycle low, not the step up.

questions.q: You can't take a 4B- unless volume dries up on the pullback into the higher low.
questions.why: False. Volume drying up there raises the grade. It's not a must. Light volume on the way down into the higher low says the sellers are mostly done, and I like seeing it. But a clean higher low and a good pause still get bought without it. On the trigger day itself, I want to see volume pick up.
questions.lesson_line: Volume drying up into the higher low raises the grade. It's not a must.
questions.simple: False. Volume drying up into the higher low raises the grade, but it's not a must.

reasons: proposed card rule, fixed before

questions.q: How much room do we want to the nearest overhead level?
choices: At least 3R
At least 1R
Any room at all
At least 10R
questions.why: At least 3R from the entry to the nearest overhead level, counting only levels above the entry.
questions.lesson_line: Three R of room, or the trade is not worth it.

wrong.At least 1R: 1R does not reach the first trim at 3R. The room has to be 3R.
wrong.Any room at all: A wall just overhead is the named mistake. We want 3R.
wrong.At least 10R: 10R is far more than the first trim needs. The line is 3R.

questions.q: A fresh reason behind the turn, like a strong earnings reaction, counts against a 4B-.
questions.why: False. It helps. A stock that turns on real news, a good earnings reaction or a guidance change, gives buyers a reason to stay. Just keep your buy out of the 3 days before the next report. A turn on news is a trade. A buy right before a report is a bet on the number.
questions.lesson_line: A fresh reason for the turn helps.
questions.simple: False. A fresh reason for the turn helps the setup, it doesn't hurt it.

reasons: the report window rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: Once you're in a 4B-, your stop only ever moves up, never down, except under the gap rule.
questions.why: True. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up. The one exception is a gap through it, where the first 30-minute low becomes the new stop. Lower it any other time and a planned small loss turns into hope. That's how small losers turn into big ones.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is the plan. It only moves up.
questions.simple: True. The stop only moves up, and the gap rule is the one exception.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4)

questions.q: Buy the open?
questions.story: The pause high is 40.00. The stock gaps open at 42.00.
choices: Pass; 5% past the pause high
Buy at market; it is so strong
Buy half size at the open
Set a limit at 40.00 and wait
questions.why: Pass. The open at 42.00 is 5% above the pause high of 40.00, and the cap is 4%. We skip a long that is already more than 4% above its trigger level. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: More than 4% past the pause high is no trade.

wrong.Buy at market; it is so strong: Past 4% the stop stays far away and the shares shrink. That is a chase.
wrong.Buy half size at the open: Half of a chase is still a chase. The line is 4%.
wrong.Set a limit at 40.00 and wait: Our entries are market orders, and the trigger already traded at the open. A resting limit at the old pause high is not the plan.

questions.simple: Pass, because 42.00 is 5% past the 40.00 pause high, and we never buy more than 4% past it.

deeper.trap: A gap above the line is not a gift. The line is 4% above the trigger level however the stock gets there, so a strong open does not move it. Skip the trade and wait for the next trigger.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)

questions.q: It's down 60% and it looks cheap. Do you buy it here?
questions.story: It's still making new lows under a falling 30-week line. No higher low yet.
choices: No, it's a plain 4B, still falling
Yes, down 60% is cheap enough
Yes, but just a starter position
Yes, it's due for a bounce
questions.answer: No, it's a plain 4B, still falling
questions.why: No. It's still making new lows, so it hasn't seen its low. That's a plain 4B, much too soon to buy. Down 60% isn't cheap, it's just down. It can lose a lot more from here. There's no level to risk against while it keeps breaking lows. I'd keep it on the radar and wait for the minus.
questions.lesson_line: Cheap isn't a reason. A falling stock is a falling stock.

wrong.Yes, down 60% is cheap enough: Buying because it looks cheap is the classic mistake. Down a lot can go further down.
wrong.Yes, but just a starter position: A smaller size doesn't fix bad timing. And we buy the full size at one price anyway.
wrong.Yes, it's due for a bounce: Due is a feeling, not a level. There's no low to risk against yet.

questions.simple: No. It's still making new lows, so it's a plain 4B, and cheap isn't a reason.

deeper.trap: Cheap is the trap. A stock down 60% and still making new lows hasn't seen its low for the cycle. The minus is the test, not the price.

reasons: x01 from one publisher plus the card's own line

questions.q: Three weeks of bounce, then today it closes under the cycle low. What's that telling you?
questions.story: It bounced for three weeks off its cycle low. Today it closed under that low.
choices: Still falling, the low wasn't the low
A bargain, buy it on the pullback
Just a longer base, still a 4B-
Noise, the low call still holds
questions.answer: Still falling, the low wasn't the low
questions.why: The low wasn't the low. A close under the cycle low means the stock never finished falling. It's back to a 4B or a plain 4. Those three weeks of bounce were just a rally in a downtrend. Take it off your 4B- list. If it builds again, the new low becomes the cycle low and you start the count over.
questions.lesson_line: A close under the cycle low resets the count.

wrong.A bargain, buy it on the pullback: There's nothing to buy. The level you'd risk against just broke.
wrong.Just a longer base, still a 4B-: A 4B- never closes under its cycle low. This one just did.
wrong.Noise, the low call still holds: We go by the close, and it closed under. That ends the call.

questions.simple: The low wasn't the low. A close under it means it's still falling, so the count resets.

deeper.counter: A close under the low ends the call, not the stock. The new low becomes the new cycle low, and the count starts over from it.

reasons: rests on the proposed card rule c35

questions.q: Buy the break?
questions.story: A 4B- shape: a higher low, a 50-day reclaim and a pause. The close is still 12% under the 200-day.
choices: No; no longs under the 200-day
Yes; the shape is perfect
Yes, on half size
questions.why: No. No longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long. Wait until price is back above it.
questions.lesson_line: The shape is not enough. The 200-day comes first.

wrong.Yes; the shape is perfect: A perfect shape under the 200-day is still under the 200-day.
wrong.Yes, on half size: Half size does not change the 200-day rule.

questions.q: You bought at 12.37 with a 12.06 stop. It just traded 13.92. How many R are you up?
questions.why: 5R. Your risk is 12.37 minus 12.06, which is 0.31 a share. The gain is 13.92 minus 12.37, which is 1.55. 1.55 over 0.31 is 5. Count in R, not dollars, so every trade reads the same whatever the price. At 5R I'm thinking about selling some into strength, especially into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. That's AMD in May 2018.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R, not dollars.
questions.simple: Divide the gain by your risk per share. Here that's 5R.

reasons: a computed key
the 5R trim is the owner's adjustable default (E51)

wrong.6.0R: You measured the gain from the stop instead of the buy.
wrong.44.9R: You divided the price by R instead of the gain.
wrong.50.0R: You slipped the decimal one place.

questions.story: A deep decline, a higher low and a 10-day pause above the 50-day. You bought the trigger.

questions.q: In a 4B-, you move the stop to breakeven as soon as you're up 1R, well before the first sell.
questions.why: False. We move it to breakeven somewhere between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell. At 1R it's too tight. A normal shake takes you out at zero, right before the move you were waiting for. Give it room to work first. Once you're up 2R or more, then think about taking the loss off the table.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven between 2R and 5R. Not at 1R.
questions.simple: False. Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R or at the first sell, not at 1R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19)

questions.q: We scanned past 4B- triggers. Which pause above the 50-day did worst at reaching 3R?
choices: A pause of 2 to 4 sessions
A pause of 5 to 10 sessions
A pause of 11 to 20 sessions
A pause of 21 to 40 sessions
questions.why: The bare 2 to 4 session pause. Only 15.7% reached 3R. The 5 to 10 session pause did best at 25.9%. A pause of a few days barely tests the 50-day, so more of them fail. A longer pause shows the line holding and builds a tighter range to trigger from. It's one scan, so I treat it as a cue. Still, I'd rather see it sit a while.
questions.lesson_line: Give the pause some days. The shortest ones did worst.

wrong.A pause of 11 to 20 sessions: 23.1% reached 3R, well ahead of the shortest pause.
wrong.A pause of 21 to 40 sessions: 21.3% reached 3R, still ahead of the shortest pause.

questions.simple: The shortest pause did worst. Give the pause some time to prove the 50-day holds.

deeper.counter: Even the best group reached 3R only about a quarter of the time, 25.9% for 5 to 10 sessions. The 11 to 20 session pause did 23.1% and 21 to 40 sessions did 21.3%. It's one scan. Use pause length as a cue, not a promise.

reasons: numbers from our own scan, which can change
rests on one dossier test
fixed before

questions.q: Your stock's 4B- looks clean. What do you want its group doing?
choices: Basing and turning up with it
Still making new lows
Doesn't matter, just the stock
One big up day, then flat
questions.answer: Basing and turning up with it
questions.why: Turning up with it. A stock rarely turns alone for long. When the group is basing and turning too, buyers are coming into the whole space and your stock has a tailwind. Fight a weak group and you own the one name swimming upstream. Pull up the group's ETF next to your chart before you buy. If the group's still sliding, I'd pass or size down.
questions.lesson_line: Check the group, not just the stock.

wrong.Still making new lows: That's buying against a weak group. Your stock fights the whole space.
wrong.Doesn't matter, just the stock: The group matters. A turn with the group behind it holds better.
wrong.One big up day, then flat: One day isn't a turn. I want the group basing and turning up.

questions.simple: You want the group turning up too. Buying against a weak group is a common mistake.

reasons: proposed card cue, not an owner ruling

questions.q: It set a higher low, then closed under it before winning back the 50-day. Where does the setup stand?
questions.story: A higher low formed weeks after the cycle low. Before the 50-day reclaim, price closed under that higher low.
choices: Off, the higher low just broke
Better, it's cheaper now
Fine, the cycle low still holds
Fine until a second close under
questions.answer: Off, the higher low just broke
questions.why: It's off. A higher low that breaks isn't a higher low anymore. That level was buyers stepping in above the old low, and they just stopped. The cycle low might still hold, but the base has to build a new higher low first. I'd leave it on the radar and wait for it to show me again.
questions.lesson_line: A higher low that breaks isn't a higher low.

wrong.Better, it's cheaper now: Cheaper isn't better. The level you'd risk against just failed.
wrong.Fine, the cycle low still holds: The cycle low holding keeps it alive, not ready. It needs a new higher low.
wrong.Fine until a second close under: One close under it is enough. It isn't a higher low anymore.

questions.simple: It's off. Once the higher low breaks, the base has to build a new one.

reasons: one cited fact only (the criteria card)
a proposed rule the owner may change
fixed before

questions.q: It closed under its cycle low, then two days later closed back over it. Is that a 4B- you can buy?
questions.story: A stock closes under its cycle low. Two sessions later it closes back over it, and you want to buy the reclaim.
choices: No, a 4B- takes weeks to build
Yes, it took the low back fast
Yes, if the volume was big
No, the 150-day has to rise first
questions.answer: No, a 4B- takes weeks to build
questions.why: No. That's an undercut and snap back, a different trade on a different clock. A 4B- never closes under its cycle low. It takes weeks to build a higher low, win back the 50-day and pause. Two days after a new low, none of that is there. If you want to trade the snap back, trade it as that setup with its own rules.

questions.q: Is that a 4B-?

choices: No; a capitulation snap back
Yes; it flushed hard to the low
Yes, if it holds the new low
No; a flush marks a Stage 2 top
questions.why: No. A capitulation buys the snap back within 3 sessions of a 2x-volume flush under every fast average. A 4B- waits weeks after the low for a higher low on drying volume and a 50-day reclaim.
questions.lesson_line: A snap back is quick. A 4B- takes weeks.

wrong.Yes; it flushed hard to the low: A flush buys the snap back. A 4B- waits for the base.
wrong.Yes, if it holds the new low: Holding the low is not enough. A 4B- waits for a higher low and a 50-day reclaim.
wrong.No; a flush marks a Stage 2 top: A flush on 2x volume under every fast average is the capitulation pattern on our card. It buys the snap back; it is not a 4B-.

questions.simple: No. This is a capitulation snap back, which is quick, while a 4B- waits weeks for a higher low.

reasons: rests on the card's lookalike line l3

questions.q: It bottomed and ran straight up into the 50-day without a single pullback. Is it a 4B- yet?
questions.story: A V off the low: straight up into the 50-day, no pullback on the way.
choices: No, it hasn't made a higher low
Yes, it's back at the 50-day
Yes, as long as volume was light
No, the 200-day isn't flat yet
questions.answer: No, it hasn't made a higher low
questions.why: Not yet. A V straight off the low has no higher low, and the higher low is the tell. It's where buyers step in above the old low on their own. Without it, the only place to risk against is the bottom, way below you. Let it pull back and hold above the cycle low. That pullback low is your higher low, and the base starts there.
questions.lesson_line: No pullback, no higher low, no 4B- yet.

wrong.Yes, it's back at the 50-day: Reaching the 50-day is one step. Without a higher low it's just a V.
wrong.Yes, as long as volume was light: Volume can't stand in for a higher low.
wrong.No, the 200-day isn't flat yet: A flat 200-day is a nice cue, not the gate. The missing piece is the higher low.

questions.simple: No. A straight run up has no pullback, so there's no higher low yet.

reasons: the higher-low numbers are the card's proposed rule

wrong.Take it, on half size: Half size does not buy more room.

Yes, and sell before the report

Yes, but only on half size
No, the 9 EMA isn't rising yet

Hold it, the stop hasn't traded
Widen the stop to give it room
Sell half and hold the rest
questions.why: Sell it. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days gets sold. The stop didn't trade, but time is its own exit. A good turn should move. If it's done nothing in two weeks, that money can work in a name that's actually going. Don't widen anything. Close it and go find the next one.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and nothing. The money has somewhere better to be.

wrong.Widen the stop to give it room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Sell half and hold the rest: The time stop sells the trade. It doesn't trim it.
wrong.Hold it, the stop hasn't traded: Time is its own exit. Under 1R after 10 days, the money goes elsewhere.

questions.q: A clean 4B- breaks its pause high above the 200-day. Our market reading just turned Red. What's the play?

choices: Stand aside, Red is mostly cash
Buy it, the base is too good
Buy full size, Red changes nothing
Short it, Red means go short
questions.answer: Stand aside, Red is mostly cash
questions.why: Stand aside. Our market reading is the app's market filter: Green, Yellow, Orange, Red. It's a guide to how much the account trades, and Red means mostly cash. Breakouts fail more often when the whole market is selling, because nothing's backing them. A great base will still be there, or set up again, when the market turns. And it's above the 200-day, so it's no short either.
questions.lesson_line: A great base in a Red market still waits.

wrong.Buy it, the base is too good: Buying against the market is how good bases turn into stop-outs. Red is mostly cash.
wrong.Buy full size, Red changes nothing: Red changes the whole account. We're mostly cash.
wrong.Short it, Red means go short: We only short below the 200-day. This one's above it.

questions.simple: Stand aside. In a Red market we're mostly cash, so even a great base waits.

questions.q: It won back the 50-day and paused a week. You haven't bought. Today it closes back under the 50-day. Now what?
questions.story: A week of pausing above the 50-day, no buy yet. Today's close is back under the line.
choices: Wait for a new pause above it
Buy the dip, it's cheaper now
Wait a day, then buy as planned
Buy the first close back over it
questions.answer: Wait for a new pause above it
questions.why: Wait for a new pause. Losing the 50-day before the trigger takes the setup off. The week above it doesn't carry over. Sellers just showed up at the line, so you want to see buyers win it back and hold there again. Once it pauses above the 50-day again, you've got a fresh high to trigger on and a fresh low to risk against.
questions.lesson_line: Lose the 50-day, wait for a fresh pause above it.

wrong.Buy the dip, it's cheaper now: A close under the 50-day is a warning, not a discount.
wrong.Wait a day, then buy as planned: The plan's off. A day of waiting isn't a new pause.
wrong.Buy the first close back over it: That's just the reclaim again. Let it pause before you buy.

questions.simple: Wait. Losing the 50-day before your buy resets it, so let it build a fresh pause.

deeper.trap: A week above the 50-day doesn't carry over. One close back under it resets the count, and you need a fresh pause above it.

reasons: one cited fact only (the criteria card)
a proposed rule the owner may change

questions.q: Your account is 50,000 and you risk 1% a trade. You buy at 22.12 with the stop at 21.49. How many shares?

The stop sets the size, never the other way around. Then check it against your position cap and take the smaller number.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.
questions.simple: Risk $500, divide by 0.63 a share, and round down. That's 793 shares.

questions.q: How do you play the open?
questions.story: You bought at 40.00 with the stop at 39.00, so 3R is 43.00. The next morning it opens at 43.60.
choices: Take a third off at the open
Wait for the close
Sell all, take the gain
Take half off at the open
questions.answer: Take a third off at the open
questions.why: Sell a third at the open. A trim level the day opens past is taken at the open. Here 43.60 is past the 3R level at 43.00. The first trim is a third at 3R, the hard rule.
questions.lesson_line: Take the trim the open hands you.

wrong.Wait for the close: The 3R level is already passed. The rule is to take the trim at the open.
wrong.Sell all, take the gain: A third at 3R. The rest waits for 5R and the trail.
wrong.Take half off at the open: The hard rule for the first trim is a third at 3R, not half. The rest waits for 5R and the trail.

questions.simple: Take a third off at the open, because the stock opened past the 3R level.

deeper.example: Entry 40.00 and stop 39.00 put 3R at 43.00. The day opens at 43.60, past the level, so the third comes off at the open price. The other two thirds wait for 5R, then the trail.

questions.q: You're long from 40.00, stop 39.00. It gaps open at 38.20 and the first 30-minute low is 37.80. What now?
questions.story: Long from 40.00, stop 39.00. Gap down open at 38.20. First 30-minute low: 37.80.
choices: Get out, the loss is past 2R
Make 37.80 the new stop
Hold it, gaps tend to fill
Sell half, keep half for a bounce
questions.answer: Get out, the loss is past 2R
questions.why: Get out. When a gap jumps your stop, the first 30-minute low becomes the new stop, but only inside 2R. Your risk was 40.00 minus 39.00, a dollar a share. Two R down is two dollars under the buy. The 37.80 low is past that. Past 2R the rule takes you out, so one bad gap can't turn into a disaster.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop has a ceiling: 2R.

wrong.Make 37.80 the new stop: The 30-minute low is the new stop only inside 2R. This one's past it.
wrong.Hold it, gaps tend to fill: Hope isn't a plan. Past 2R you're out.
wrong.Sell half, keep half for a bounce: The gap rule has no half exit. Past 2R, all of it goes.

questions.simple: Get out. The first 30-minute low is past 2R, so it can't be your new stop.

deeper.example: Long from 40.00, stop 39.00. It gaps to 38.20 and the first 30-minute low is 37.80. That low is more than 2R down, past the ceiling, so it can't be the new stop. Had it held inside 2R, it would have been.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)

questions.q: What now?
questions.story: You hold the last third of a fast mover after both trims. Today it closes under its 10-day.

Hold until the 50-day breaks down
Move the stop down to the 50-day
questions.answer: Sell the last third on that close
questions.why: Sell the last third. A fast mover trails the 10-day, and we sell on a close below it.
questions.lesson_line: The trail is a close under the 10-day. Sell it.

wrong.Hold until the 50-day breaks down: The trail is the 10-day for a fast mover, not the 50-day.
wrong.Move the stop down to the 50-day: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.

questions.q: Your 4B- is working. A friend tells you to buy more shares on each higher low. What do you tell him?
questions.story: The trade is up and working. Your friend adds along the way and says you should too.
choices: No, one price and one stop
Sure, add on each higher low
Sure, but add half the size
No, sell half to lock it in
questions.answer: No, one price and one stop
questions.why: No. We buy the full size at one price with one stop. An add on every higher low makes adding a routine, and that's not how we trade. Every add is a higher price with its own risk. Your average cost climbs, and one pullback can wipe out the gain on the whole thing. Adding to a working winner does happen, but it's rare and a feel call, never the plan. The trade grows by being right and riding the trail.
questions.lesson_line: Full size once. Adding on every higher low isn't the plan.

wrong.Sure, add on each higher low: That makes adding a routine. Your cost climbs with every add.
wrong.Sure, but add half the size: A smaller add is still a planned add, a second price and a second stop.
wrong.No, sell half to lock it in: That's a different call. The first sell is a judgment, into a push on day 3 or later.

questions.simple: No, we buy once, full size, with one stop. An add to a winner is rare, never a routine.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5)

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You are up 4R in four days on a vertical, wide-range burst.
choices: Sell a big part into the burst
Add; it is going parabolic
Hold it all; the trail will handle it
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the burst
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. A climax run on your own long is for selling into; how much is a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: A vertical burst is for selling into.

wrong.Add; it is going parabolic: Adding is the named mistake, and a burst is for selling into.
wrong.Hold it all; the trail will handle it: The trail catches the turn late. A burst is the moment to bank a big part.

questions.q: On a stock we really like, our position can be as big as 5% of its average daily volume.
questions.why: False. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. Past that, you are the volume. Getting out on a bad day means pushing the price down against yourself. And if a stock is so thin that 1% is a small position, it's not one we should even be watching.
questions.lesson_line: Size to the stock's volume, not just your stop.
questions.simple: False. We cap a position at 1% of the stock's average daily volume.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)

Wait; the market must make a new high
Go all in on this one
No change; judge the stock alone

questions.why: Good conditions. The card says the best turns come after a broad market decline, once the market itself turns back up. After a correction, start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones work.
questions.lesson_line: A market turning up is the wind behind the turn.

wrong.Wait; the market must make a new high: The best turns come when the market itself turns back up, not after a new high.
wrong.Go all in on this one: After a correction, start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones work.
wrong.No change; judge the stock alone: The market matters. The card wants a Green or Yellow reading, and it says the best turns come once the market itself turns back up.

questions.q: Your 4B- stalls after the buy and drifts back toward the old low. A friend says hold it as an investment. What do you do?
questions.story: A few days after the buy it stalls and starts drifting back toward the cycle low. The stop hasn't traded yet.
choices: Sell it by the plan, it's a trade
Hold it, it's a long-term bottom
Add shares, it's cheaper here
Lower the stop to give it room
questions.answer: Sell it by the plan, it's a trade
questions.why: Sell it by the plan. A 4B- is a swing trade, days to a few weeks. It exits on its stop or its time stop, not by getting promoted to an investment. Riding a failed turn back down into Stage 4 is how one small loss becomes the worst trade of your year. The stop is there. Let it do its job.
questions.lesson_line: Don't turn a trade into an investment.

wrong.Hold it, it's a long-term bottom: That's the mistake: riding a failed trade back into Stage 4.
wrong.Add shares, it's cheaper here: That's adding to a loser, and we never do that. One price, one stop.
wrong.Lower the stop to give it room: The stop only moves up. Lowering it turns a planned loss into hope.

questions.simple: Sell by the plan. A 4B- is a short trade, and we never ride one back into Stage 4.

deeper.trap: The friend's story sounds patient, but it changes the trade. A 4B- is a short-term play, and a stalled one exits on the stop or the time stop. Hope isn't an exit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)
fixed before

questions.q: You bought this 4B- at 12.99 with a 12.59 stop. The next day traded 12.48 and took you out. How do you grade it?
questions.story: A 37.5% decline, a higher low and a 12-day pause, then the trigger. The buy day closed near its high.
choices: A planned loss, the stop worked
The stop was set too tight
The buy came in too late
Proof the 4B- doesn't work
questions.answer: A planned loss, the stop worked
questions.why: A planned loss. You bought the trigger, your stop sat a few cents under the low of the day, and it cost you 3.1%. That's inside the 5% we accept. 12.48 traded under 12.59 and the stop did exactly what it's for. Judge the plan, not the outcome. Take enough good setups and some will do this. That was F in February 2024.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out can be the plan working.

wrong.The stop was set too tight: It sat a few cents under the low of the day, where it belongs. Calling it tight after the fact is how stops get widened.
wrong.The buy came in too late: You bought the trigger, right through the pause high. That's not a chase.
wrong.Proof the 4B- doesn't work: One loss proves nothing. This setup loses often and gets paid on its runners.

questions.simple: It was a planned loss. The stop did its job and kept the loss small.

deeper.trap: A stop-out isn't proof of a bad setup. The next session's low of 12.48 was under the 12.59 stop, so the exit happened as planned. Don't widen a stop after the fact. It only moves up.

questions.q: You got stopped out the next day for 1.4%. When do you buy this stock again?

Right away, it's the same setup
Only below your first buy price
After waiting a full week

questions.simple: Buy again only if it triggers again, as a brand new trade with its own stop.

The pause was too long
The base was too short

choices: The market reading
A tighter stop
A bigger position

questions.q: It's down 34% from its high and turning. Is it a 4B-?

Yes, 34% is deep enough
Yes, it sat under the 150-day
No, it's a plain 4B, still falling

wrong.Yes, it sat under the 150-day: Under it is half the picture. The line also has to be falling, and it was rising.
wrong.No, it's a plain 4B, still falling: There's no Stage 4 here to be late in. The 150-day was rising.

questions.simple: No. The 150-day was rising at the low, so it's a pullback in an uptrend, not a Stage 4 turn.

deeper.trap: Depth fools people. A 34% drop looks like a Stage 4, but the 150-day tells the stage. Read it at the low. If it was rising, this is a pullback in an uptrend.

questions.q: Two days off its cycle low it pops 4.1%, then dips to a low 3.5% above it. Is that your higher low?
questions.story: Two days off its cycle low it pops 4.1%. Then it slips back to a low 3.5% above the cycle low.
choices: Not yet, that's just chop at the low
Yes, it's above the cycle low
Yes, any low over the bottom counts
Yes, buy it as it turns up
questions.answer: Not yet, that's just chop at the low
questions.why: Not yet. Two days and a 4.1% pop isn't a base. Price is still sitting on the low. A real higher low comes after buyers lift it clear off the bottom, then a pullback that holds. On a 4B- that takes weeks, not days. It's a read by eye, not a fixed percent. Here there's nothing to pull back from yet, so I'd wait for it to show me more.
questions.lesson_line: A higher low needs a real rally before it.

wrong.Yes, it's above the cycle low: Above the low isn't enough. There was no real rally for it to pull back from.
wrong.Yes, any low over the bottom counts: A wiggle isn't a step up. You want a clear rally, then a pullback that holds.
wrong.Yes, buy it as it turns up: There's no base to buy yet. It's still sitting on the low.

questions.simple: Not yet. A quick pop and a dip right on the low is chop, not a higher low.

deeper.trap: The dip held above the low, so it looks like a step up. But a pop of a couple of days and a slip right back is chop on the low. Read the shape: a real rally, then a pullback that holds.

questions.q: It's 2022-07-18 and the stock is back over its 50-day. It reports after tomorrow's close. Can you buy it here?
questions.story: It closed back over its 50-day on 2022-07-15 and again on 2022-07-18. The company reports after the close on 2022-07-19.
choices: No, it's too close to the report
Yes, the reclaim was clean
Yes, it's before the report
No, wait for the 200-day first

The report can gap it right through your stop, and a stop can't catch a gap. Even without the report, a close back over the 50-day isn't the buy. You wait for the pause and the trigger. Check the report date in our app's calendar before every buy. This was NFLX in July 2022.
questions.lesson_line: Check the report date before every buy, even on a clean chart.

wrong.Yes, the reclaim was clean: A clean chart doesn't move the earnings window.
wrong.Yes, it's before the report: Right before the report is exactly when we don't buy.
wrong.No, wait for the 200-day first: The problem here is the report date, not the 200-day.

questions.simple: No. A buy on the 18th is the day before the report, and we don't buy within 3 days of one.

deeper.trap: A clean chart isn't a free pass. The window looks at the report date, not at how good the base looks. Check the date before every buy.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)
fixed before

questions.q: It's trading through the pause high right now. What's your plan?
questions.story: 78 sessions off a December low, a February higher low, then a 19-day pause above a turning 50-day.
choices: Buy 49.99, stop 49.05, sell day 3+
Buy 49.99, stop 45.00, hold it all
Skip it, wait for a Stage 2 break
Buy 49.99, stop 49.05, add on dips
questions.why: Buy 49.99 at market, stop 49.05. That's a tight 1.9% stop. The first sell is a judgment, into a push on day 3 or later. Then trail what's left under the 9 or 20 EMA. One price, one stop, and no add in the plan. Write it all down before the open: entry, stop and size. Then you're just executing. That's NUS in April 2013.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, size, first sell, trail. Write it before the open.

wrong.Buy 49.99, stop 45.00, hold it all: 45.00 is a wide stop pulled from nowhere. The honest one sat 1.9% away, and there's no plan to sell.
wrong.Skip it, wait for a Stage 2 break: That's a different trade, later. You're looking at the 4B- buy.
wrong.Buy 49.99, stop 49.05, add on dips: Right entry and stop, then adding on dips breaks it. One price, one stop.

questions.simple: Buy at market through the pause high with the stop at 49.05, and sell some on day 3 or later.

deeper.example: NUS had a December low, a February higher low, three months of flat 150- and 200-day lines, then a 19-day pause above a turning 50-day. The buy was 49.99 with the stop at 49.05, 1.9% away.

reasons: numbers read from our own bars (dossier)
entry trigger rests on held decision D-003
stop width rests on held decision D-005

questions.q: Two 4B- breaks trigger today. Which one gets the bigger size?
questions.story: A: a clean higher low on light volume, a tight pause on a flat 50-day, group and market turning up. B: a 50-day still falling steeply, group and market not turning.
choices: A, the stronger base and backdrop
B, a steep 50-day has more upside
Same size, both broke the high
Neither, the stop sets the size
questions.answer: A, the stronger base and backdrop
questions.why: A. Everything lines up behind it. Volume dried up into the higher low, the pause is tight on a flat 50-day, and the group and market are turning with it. I'd call that the A+ end, and A+ gets sized up. B is still fighting a steeply falling 50-day with no help from the group or the market. That's a B- at best, sized down. Same trigger, different odds.
questions.lesson_line: Same trigger, different grade. The grade sets the size.

wrong.B, a steep 50-day has more upside: A steeply falling 50-day is a weak cue. B- or lower gets sized down.
wrong.Same size, both broke the high: The break is the same. What's behind it isn't, and the grade sets the size.
wrong.Neither, the stop sets the size: The stop sets the shares for your risk. The grade sets how much you risk.

questions.simple: A gets the bigger size. Its base and backdrop are strong, and B's are weak.

deeper.trap: Both broke the pause high, so both look the same on a screen. The difference is what sits behind the break. A clean base and a rising backdrop earn size. A weak base earns less.

reasons: grades rest on card judgment with no stated thresholds
the flat 50-day number is held (D-070)
fixed before

questions.q: You take five 4B- trades by the rules. Four stop out and one runs 5R. How do you read that?
questions.story: Five trades, all by the plan. Four small stops. One runner to 5R.
choices: Normal, this setup loses often
Broken, the setup doesn't work
Wrong stops, they should be wider
Bad luck, good setups win most
questions.why: Normal. In our scan of past 4B- triggers above the 200-day, 22.2% of 1,110 hits reached 3R and 13.9% reached 5R. Most never got to 3R. So four stops in five is an ordinary run for this setup. Four small stops and one 5R runner still nets you a gain. The losses stay small at the stop and the runners pay for them. Judge it over many trades, not five.
questions.lesson_line: Most 4B- trades don't reach 3R. Judge it over many trades.

wrong.Broken, the setup doesn't work: Four stops in five fits what we measured. Only 22.2% reached 3R.
wrong.Wrong stops, they should be wider: Our stop sits a few cents under the low of the day, set before the buy. Widening it just shrinks your shares.
wrong.Bad luck, good setups win most: This setup doesn't win most. It wins big when it works.

questions.simple: That's normal. Most 4B- trades never reach 3R, so four stops in five is ordinary.

deeper.counter: The hit rate alone says little. Winners get sold into strength and each loss is held to the stop. Judge the setup over many trades, not five.

reasons: a statistic from our own test that can change
one cited fact only (our scan)
rests on the 200-day treatment held in D-009
fixed before

questions.q: In Bulkowski's own trades, Stage 4 buys made money about 24% of the time.
questions.why: True. Bulkowski's own Stage 4 buys made money 24% of the time, so a 4B- is a low-hit-rate trade that lives on small stops and trims.
questions.lesson_line: Buying near a Stage 4 low is a low-odds trade. Trade it small and short.

questions.q: A washout low, a higher low, and now a pause over the 50-day. Do you take this one?
choices: Take it, it's above the 200-day
Pass, the 200-day is overhead
Pass, there's no real higher low
Take it, washouts always bounce
questions.why: Take it. A spring washout, a higher low well above it, and an 11-day pause that walked up through the 50, 150 and 200-day lines. The close before the trigger was above the 200-day, so it clears our hard line. It went in with a 2% stop and ran to 5R in 9 sessions. That's DY in May 2025. One winner proves nothing, but that's the picture you want.
questions.lesson_line: The 200-day first, then the base. Both pass here.

wrong.Pass, the 200-day is overhead: Look again. Price is above the 200-day here.
wrong.Pass, there's no real higher low: Look again. The second low sits well above the washout.
wrong.Take it, washouts always bounce: A washout alone isn't a setup, and nothing always bounces. This one has the higher low and the pause.

questions.simple: Take it. The close was above the 200-day, and the base has a higher low and a pause.

deeper.trap: A clean win is a bad teacher. The same shape lost in other cases, like F and META, both stopped the next session. Judge the process, not the one hit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)
figures read from our own daily bars
fixed before

questions.q: A 50% decline, a 12% higher low and a 50-day reclaim. The shape looks right. Can you take it?
choices: Pass, it's still under the 200-day
Take it, the base is textbook
Take it, the higher low is big
Pass, it's a plain 4B, still falling
questions.why: Pass. The close the day before the trigger was 10.2% under the 200-day. The decline, the higher low and the reclaim can all be right, and it's still not ours. Below the 200-day is a hard no for stocks. Under it, every rally runs into holders who want out. Only indexes and levered ETFs get an exception. That's BAC in June 2020.
questions.lesson_line: The shape isn't enough. For a stock, the 200-day decides.

wrong.Take it, the base is textbook: A good-looking base doesn't matter with the close under the 200-day. That line comes first.
wrong.Take it, the higher low is big: A big higher low doesn't lift the close over the 200-day.
wrong.Pass, it's a plain 4B, still falling: The higher low and the 50-day reclaim put it past a plain 4B. The reason to pass is the 200-day.

questions.simple: Pass. The close is still under the 200-day, and we don't buy stocks under it.

deeper.trap: The shape looks complete. A 50% decline, a 12% higher low and a 50-day reclaim, and the close was still 10% under the 200-day. Check the 200-day before you admire the base.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26) and held decision D-009
numbers read from our own bars (dossier)

questions.q: Four names on your list this morning. Which one is still a 4B- candidate?
questions.story: A: still making new lows. B: the close is under the 200-day. C: a higher low, a pause over the 50-day, open room overhead. D: reports in 2 days.
choices: A, still making new lows
B, close under the 200-day
C, higher low and a pause
D, reports in two days
questions.answer: C, higher low and a pause
questions.why: C. Run every name through the checks. A is a plain 4B, still falling. B is under the 200-day, a hard no. D reports in 2 days, inside our 3-day window. C has the higher low, the pause and room over its head. It still has to trigger through the pause high, and you skip it if it's more than 4% past that.
questions.lesson_line: Run every check. One failure ends it.

wrong.A, still making new lows: Still making new lows is a plain 4B, much too soon to buy.
wrong.B, close under the 200-day: Under the 200-day, no longs. That's a hard line.
wrong.D, reports in two days: A report inside 3 days ends it for now.

questions.simple: C. The other three each fail a check: a plain 4B, under the 200-day, and a report too soon.

deeper.trap: C only survived the list. It still needs the close above the 200-day, the 50-day won back and a trade through the pause high. Then the buy can't be more than 4% past the trigger.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22, B26)
the 3R room number is the card's proposal

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: After a correction, start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones ___.
questions.why: Work. After a correction, start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones work. Add positions, not shares to one trade.
questions.lesson_line: Start small after a correction. Let the first positions earn the next ones.
questions.simple: Start small after a correction and add more only as the first ones work.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F68)

questions.q: The reading turned Green after a broad selloff. Your first two 4B- trades are working. A third triggers. Do you take it?
questions.story: A broad selloff ends and the market reading turns Green. You hold two 4B- trades, both up and past their first sell. A third 4B- triggers today.
choices: Yes, the first two are working
No, wait for a new index high
Yes, by adding to the first two
No, three at once is too many
questions.answer: Yes, the first two are working
questions.why: Yes. After a correction we start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones work. Yours are working, and that's the market telling you the turn is real. So the third goes on as a new trade with its own stop. That's adding positions, not adding to a trade. Let the market earn your exposure.
questions.lesson_line: Add positions, not shares. Let the first ones prove the turn.

wrong.Yes, by adding to the first two: That's adding to a trade, not a new position. The third name goes on with its own stop.
wrong.No, wait for a new index high: We start as the reading turns Green again. Waiting for a new index high means missing the turn.
wrong.No, three at once is too many: Start with a few and add as they work. They're working, so the third is the plan.

questions.simple: Yes. The first two are working, so you add a new position with its own stop.

deeper.counter: Add positions, not shares. A third name spreads the plan across trades. Adding to a winner means a second price and a second stop. We buy one price with one stop, and an add is rare, never the plan.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F68)
fixed before

questions.q: Two stocks in a basing group, same higher low, same pause. A won back its 50-day early, B weeks later. Which do you favor?
questions.story: The group is basing. Both stocks show the same higher low and pause above the 50-day. A reclaimed its 50-day in the group's first week of turning. B reclaimed it weeks later, after most of the group.
choices: A, it turned with the leaders
B, it waited for the group
Neither, the order doesn't matter
Both the same, the group's basing
questions.answer: A, it turned with the leaders
questions.why: A. When a group turns, the first names to win back their 50-day are where buyers go first. That's leadership showing up early. B came weeks later, after most of the group, so it's following. It's a cue, not a deal breaker, and B can still be a fine setup. But if I'm picking one, I want the one that led.
questions.lesson_line: In a turning group, favor the first to win back the 50-day.

wrong.B, it waited for the group: B is following. The cue goes to the names that turn first.
wrong.Neither, the order doesn't matter: The order is the cue. The early ones are where buyers go first.
wrong.Both the same, the group's basing: A basing group is half of it. The other half is your stock turning among the first.

questions.simple: A. It won back its 50-day among the first in its group, and that's a sign of leadership.

deeper.trap: Being late isn't a veto. It's a cue, not a gate, so B can still be a fine setup. It just doesn't earn this cue.

reasons: one cited fact only (the criteria card)

questions.q: You're grading a 4B-. What do you want the 150-day and 200-day lines doing over the trade?
choices: Flat, or starting to turn
Still falling steeply
Doesn't matter for the grade
The 150 crossing the 200
questions.why: Flat or turning. Lines that have gone flat mean the selling that dragged them down has dried up. Steeply falling lines overhead mean sellers are still in charge, and every rally runs into them. NUS had flat 150 and 200-day lines for months before its run. It's a cue for the grade, not a rule. I'd size up the flat one and size down the steep one.
questions.lesson_line: Flat long averages beat falling ones.

wrong.Still falling steeply: That's the weaker picture. Sellers are still pressing those lines down.
wrong.Doesn't matter for the grade: It counts. Flat or turning lines are the better grade.
wrong.The 150 crossing the 200: A cross isn't what you're grading. You want both lines flat or turning.

questions.simple: Flat or turning long averages are the better picture. A steep fall is the weaker one.

reasons: the card cue plus one web quote (x11) from a page that could not be re-opened
proposed card cue

questions.q: Price is above the 200-day, but the 200-day is still falling steeply. That alone cancels the 4B-.
questions.why: False. A steeply falling 200-day is a weaker picture, not a veto. It lowers the grade, so I'd size it down. The hard line is where price sits. Price above the 200-day passes, and price under it ends the trade for a stock, whatever the slope. MSFT in May 2001 triggered with the 200-day still falling and stopped out 7 sessions later.
questions.lesson_line: A falling long average lowers the grade. Price under the 200-day ends it.
questions.simple: False. A falling 200-day lowers the grade, but only price under the line ends it.

deeper.counter: A cue isn't a gate, but a gate sits right beside it. A 200-day can fall and still sit under price. If price is under it, no longs, whatever the cue says.

reasons: proposed card cue
x11 quote from a page that could not be re-opened

questions.q: Pre-market, your 4B- trades through its 20.00 pause high. The open is an hour away. Do you buy now?
questions.story: Pause high 20.00. Pre-market prints are already above it. The bell is an hour off.
choices: No, wait for regular hours
Yes, with a market order
Yes, with a limit at 20.00
No, wait a day to see it hold
questions.why: No. We don't buy outside regular hours. Pre-market is thin, a few shares can print through the high, and the open can look nothing like it. Wait for the bell. If it trades through 20.00 in regular hours, that's your market order. Have the alert set so you're ready.
questions.lesson_line: Regular hours only. A pre-market print isn't a buy.

wrong.Yes, with a market order: Right order type, wrong time. Pre-market is outside regular hours.
wrong.Yes, with a limit at 20.00: We buy with a market order, and pre-market is outside regular hours.
wrong.No, wait a day to see it hold: No need to wait a day. Buy it at market if it trades through 20.00 after the open.

questions.simple: No. We only buy in regular hours, so buy it if it trades through 20.00 after the open.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, E58)
the trigger itself is the card's default

questions.q: The low of the day is 25.00 even, a round number. Where does your stop go?
choices: A few cents under 25.00
Right on 25.00
A few cents over 25.00
A full dollar under 25.00
questions.why: A few cents under 25.00. Our stop goes a few cents under the low of the day, never right on it. On a round number that matters even more. Round numbers are where everyone parks stops, and where buyers often step in. Sit right on it and a quick dip to the number tags you before the bounce. Then size off that stop.
questions.lesson_line: A few cents under the round number, never right on it.

wrong.Right on 25.00: A quick tag of the round number takes you out right before the bounce.
wrong.A few cents over 25.00: That's above the level. Your stop goes under it.
wrong.A full dollar under 25.00: That widens your risk for nothing and shrinks your size.

questions.simple: A few cents under 25.00. Right on a round number, a quick dip takes you out.

reasons: proposed card line c42 plus the rulebook's default stop (A3)

questions.q: Our card puts the stop right on the nearest round number.
questions.why: False. The card says not on a round number: a few cents under it. The default stop for a long is a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low.
questions.lesson_line: A few cents under the round number, not on it.
questions.simple: False. Our stop sits a few cents under a round number, not right on it.

reasons: one cited fact only (the criteria card)

questions.q: You buy a 4B- and plan to sell by hand if it breaks your stop level. Nothing's entered with your broker. What's wrong?
questions.story: The stop is a number on your notepad. No order sits with the broker.
choices: You need a real stop order in
Nothing, you'll be at the screen
An alert's enough if you're fast
Enter it after the first sell
questions.answer: You need a real stop order in
questions.why: You need a real stop order. A stop in your head isn't a stop. You'll be in a meeting, the wifi drops, or you talk yourself into one more day. The broker doesn't hesitate. Enter it the moment you're filled, and only ever move it up.
questions.lesson_line: Place the order. A stop in your head isn't a stop.

wrong.Nothing, you'll be at the screen: Watching isn't an order. The broker's stop works when you look away.
wrong.An alert's enough if you're fast: An alert isn't an order. Fast still means a choice, and choices hesitate.
wrong.Enter it after the first sell: Stop first. It goes in the moment you're filled.

questions.simple: Put in a real stop order with your broker. A stop in your head isn't a stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D41)

questions.q: Our stop is a real order with the broker, and it only moves up.
questions.why: True. A real stop order with the broker, and it only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Real order, with the broker. It only moves up.

questions.q: On a steadier mover, you trail what's left under the 20 EMA rather than the 9 EMA.
questions.why: True. Fast movers get the 9 EMA, steadier ones the 20 EMA. A steady mover dips to its 9 all the time without breaking trend, so a 9 EMA trail shakes you out early. The 20 gives it room. Either way you sell what's left on a close below the line, not an intraday poke.
questions.lesson_line: Fast mover, 9 EMA. Steadier mover, 20 EMA.
questions.simple: True. Steadier movers trail the 20 EMA and fast movers the 9 EMA, sold on a close below.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E52)

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You hold two thirds after the 3R trim. In three days the stock goes parabolic, 4.5R up and far over its 10-day.
choices: Sell a big part of it into the move
Hold it all until a 10-day close
Add to it while it keeps running
Wait for a red day, then sell some
questions.answer: Sell a big part of it into the move
questions.why: Sell a big part into the burst. A climax run on your own long is sold into, and how much is a judgment call. Do not add: one price, one stop, no adding along the way.
questions.lesson_line: A parabolic burst is for selling into. How much is your call.

wrong.Hold it all until a 10-day close: The trail catches the turn late. A parabolic burst is the moment to sell a big part.
wrong.Add to it while it keeps running: No adding along the way: one price, one stop. A burst is for selling into.
wrong.Wait for a red day, then sell some: The card says sell a big part into the run, not after it turns.

questions.simple: Sell a big part into the burst, since a climax run is for selling into.

deeper.trap: The trail feels safe because it is a rule, but it fires on a close under the 10-day, after the burst has run. The burst is the moment to bank a big part. The trail then handles what is left.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C34, a judgment call)

questions.q: The pause high is 40.00. It gaps open at 42.00, 5% over it. Do you buy the open?
questions.story: Pause high 40.00. Today it gaps open at 42.00, 5% above the trigger.
choices: Pass, it's already too far up
Buy at market, it's strong
Buy half size at the open
Set a limit at 40.00 and wait
questions.answer: Pass, it's already too far up
questions.why: Pass on the open. 42.00 is two dollars over the 40.00 pause high, 5% past it. We don't buy more than 4% over the trigger. Chasing costs you size. Your stop doesn't move up with the gap, so the distance grows and your shares shrink for the same risk. There's one more way in. If it flushes back in the morning and curls up inside that 4%, you can buy the curl at market.
questions.simple: Pass. At 42.00 it's 5% past the 40.00 pause high, and we never buy more than 4% past it.
questions.lesson_line: More than 4% past the trigger is no trade.

wrong.Buy half size at the open: Half a chase is still a chase.
wrong.Set a limit at 40.00 and wait: Not a resting limit. If it flushes back and curls up inside the 4%, you buy that curl at market.
wrong.Buy at market, it's strong: Strong and stretched. Past 4% your stop's far away and your shares shrink.

deeper.trap: A gap over the line isn't a gift. The 4% line holds however the stock gets there, so a strong open doesn't move it. A morning flush that curls back up inside it is the one way in.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)
replaces q21

questions.q: You'd buy at 50.00 with a 48.50 stop. The falling 150-day sits at 52.00, just overhead. Do you take it?
questions.story: Your risk is 1.50 a share. The falling 150-day sits at 52.00, 2.00 above your buy. The 200-day is below you.
choices: Pass, the wall's right overhead
Take it, the 150-day will break
Take it, it's over the 200-day
Pass, no longs under the 150-day
questions.why: Pass. You're risking 1.50 to make 2.00 before you hit a falling 150-day. That line is where the last buyers sit on losses, waiting to get out even. It'll likely stall there. I want room to run, a few R at least, before the first wall. Here there's barely more than one. Wait for it to get through the line and set up again.
questions.simple: Pass. The falling 150-day is just overhead, so there's barely any room to run.
questions.lesson_line: A wall just overhead is no trade. Count the room.

wrong.Take it, the 150-day will break: Maybe, maybe not. Hoping through a falling line isn't room.
wrong.Take it, it's over the 200-day: That clears one gate, not the room. The wall is 2.00 away.
wrong.Pass, no longs under the 150-day: Our hard line is the 200-day, not the 150. The problem here is room.

reasons: a proposed number the owner may change
replaces q33

questions.q: You're up 4R, still holding two thirds. Three straight up days, the last two on gap ups, range and volume growing. What's the play?
questions.story: Up 4R with two thirds left. Three up days in a row. The last two opened on gap ups. Range and volume grew each day.
choices: Sell a big part into the run
Hold it all, let the trail work
Add a little while it's strong
Wait for 5R, then decide
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the run
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. Up days in a row, gap ups, wider ranges, rising volume. That's a parabolic burst, the kind of last leg that often marks the top of the move. How much you sell is a judgment. The trail only sells on a close under the line, and by then a burst can give a lot back. Sell into the strength while buyers are paying up.
questions.lesson_line: Up days, gaps, wider ranges, rising volume: sell into that burst.

wrong.Hold it all, let the trail work: The trail sells only on a close under its line. A burst can give back a lot before then.
wrong.Add a little while it's strong: Never into a burst like this. A burst is for selling into, not buying.
wrong.Wait for 5R, then decide: The burst is the signal, not the R count. Sell into it while it's here.

questions.simple: Sell a big part into it. A burst of up days, gaps and rising volume is for selling into.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C34, a judgment call)
the burst signs are B26's parabolic burst, read as the climax run C34 names
